variants.title: Size the cache
variants.context: The target is 1.5 million operations per second with an 80/20 read-write mix, a 2 TB working set, RF=2, and 48 GB usable memory per node.
variants.prompt: 1.5 million operations per second with 80% reads. How many reads per second?
variants.explanation: 1.5M × 0.80 = 1.2M reads per second; writes are the remaining 300K.

variants.title: Size the cache
variants.context: The target is 1.5 million operations per second with an 80/20 read-write mix, a 2 TB working set, RF=2, and 48 GB usable memory per node.
variants.prompt: 1.2 million reads per second at a 90% hit rate. How many reads per second reach the origin?
variants.hint: Multiply reads by the miss rate.
variants.explanation: 1.2M × 0.10 = 120K origin reads per second; the origin must survive that plus a recovery surge.

variants.title: Size the cache
variants.context: The target is 1.5 million operations per second with an 80/20 read-write mix, a 2 TB working set, RF=2, and 48 GB usable memory per node.
variants.prompt: A 2 TB working set with RF=2 on nodes with 48 GB usable memory each. What is the memory-only node floor?
variants.hint: Double the working set, then divide by usable memory and round up.
variants.explanation: 2 TB × 2 = 4,000 GB; 4,000 ÷ 48 = 83.3, so 84 nodes before skew, failure, and rebalancing headroom.

mistakes.feedback: Round up; 83 nodes hold less than 4 TB.

variants.title: State the cache contract
variants.context: A distributed cache is not authoritative storage. Decide which values may be stale or lost, which namespaces need read-your-writes, and what happens when the cache is unavailable. No cross-key transactions; values above 1 MB belong elsewhere.
variants.prompt: A value exists only in the cache and nowhere else. What is this system?
options: A cache, because reads reach the value with a normal GET.
A hot cache, because that key has a 100 percent hit rate.
A database with a durability problem, not a cache.
optionFeedback: The access shape is not what makes something a cache; a cache holds copies of data that lives somewhere else.
Hit rate says nothing about durability. Losing the only copy still loses the data.
Is the cache disposable? If not, it is authoritative storage.
variants.hint: What happens if the value is lost?
variants.explanation: Locks, balances, and durable counters remain outside the cache contract.

variants.title: State the cache contract
variants.context: A distributed cache is not authoritative storage. Decide which values may be stale or lost, which namespaces need read-your-writes, and what happens when the cache is unavailable. No cross-key transactions; values above 1 MB belong elsewhere.
variants.prompt: Session state must be read back immediately after it is written in the same region. Which promise?
options: No promise; the client re-reads until the session appears.
Read-your-writes within the serving region for the session namespace.
Eventual consistency up to 100 ms, as for derived objects.
optionFeedback: A retry loop hides the gap instead of closing it, and a user who lands on a miss is logged out.
Namespaces carry different staleness budgets.
Derived objects tolerate a 100 ms window. A session read that lands inside it fails authentication.
variants.hint: What is the staleness budget for this namespace?
variants.explanation: State one namespace contract at a time.

variants.title: State the cache contract
variants.context: A distributed cache is not authoritative storage. Decide which values may be stale or lost, which namespaces need read-your-writes, and what happens when the cache is unavailable. No cross-key transactions; values above 1 MB belong elsewhere.
variants.prompt: A client wants to update two keys atomically. What does the contract say?
options: No cross-key transaction guarantee; use single-key operations.
Supported by MGET, which touches both keys in one round trip.
Supported by holding a lock key while both writes are issued.
optionFeedback: Cross-key atomicity is out of scope.
MGET batches reads and returns per-key results. It never makes two writes atomic.
A lock key can be evicted at any moment, so it cannot make two writes atomic.
variants.hint: Which operations does the cache promise?
variants.explanation: GET, SET, DELETE, and MGET with per-key results.

variants.title: Bound the miss
variants.context: A miss must not become an unlimited request to the backing store: request coalescing, origin admission limits, TTL jitter, and stale-value policies bound the miss path.
variants.prompt: A popular key expires and ten thousand requests miss at once. Which control prevents ten thousand origin reads?
options: Request coalescing, so one origin read serves the waiters.
Provisioning the origin for the full miss burst.
A shorter TTL so fewer requests pile up on one expiry.
optionFeedback: Coalescing collapses simultaneous misses.
Capacity sized for the burst still pays ten thousand reads. It moves the cost rather than removing it.
A shorter TTL expires the key more often, so the same stampede happens more frequently.
variants.hint: How many origin reads does one missing key deserve?

variants.title: Bound the miss
variants.context: A miss must not become an unlimited request to the backing store: request coalescing, origin admission limits, TTL jitter, and stale-value policies bound the miss path.
variants.prompt: Thousands of keys were written at the same second and will expire together. Which control helps?
options: Synchronized expiry so every copy refreshes together.
Removing TTLs so the keys never expire together.
TTL jitter that spreads expirations over a window.
optionFeedback: Refreshing together is exactly the wave you are trying to avoid.
Without TTLs nothing refreshes, so the cache serves unbounded stale data.
Jitter prevents synchronized expiration waves.
variants.hint: When do these keys expire relative to each other?

variants.title: Bound the miss
variants.context: A miss must not become an unlimited request to the backing store: request coalescing, origin admission limits, TTL jitter, and stale-value policies bound the miss path.
variants.prompt: The cache tier fails entirely. What protects the origin?
options: Client retries with backoff until the cache tier returns.
Origin admission limits with a defined degraded response.
Nothing; the origin serves the full read volume directly.
optionFeedback: Retries add load to the only tier still serving, so they amplify the outage.
Cache loss must not become an origin outage.
The origin was never sized for the cached read volume, so unbounded fallback takes it down too.
variants.hint: What is the origin fallback budget?
variants.explanation: Define origin deadlines, retry budgets, and degradation before choosing software.

variants.title: Own the key
variants.context: For one ring version, each key has deterministic primary ownership. Fenced ownership, gradual range movement, replica promotion, and warm-up controls make membership changes observable and reversible.
variants.prompt: Two nodes both believe they own a key range during a migration. Which control prevents conflicting writes?
options: Fenced ownership tied to the ring version.
More virtual nodes so each moved range is smaller.
Faster gossip so membership converges sooner.
optionFeedback: Only one owner per ring version, enforced by fencing.
Smaller ranges shrink the disputed keyspace, but both nodes still accept writes inside it.
Faster convergence narrows the overlap window; it never closes it.
variants.hint: What proves which node owns the range now?
variants.explanation: Membership changes must be observable and reversible.

variants.title: Own the key
variants.context: For one ring version, each key has deterministic primary ownership. Fenced ownership, gradual range movement, replica promotion, and warm-up controls make membership changes observable and reversible.
variants.prompt: Replicas of a shard sit on the same host. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; two copies of the shard exist.
They should move to one rack so replication stays fast.
They share a failure unit instead of spanning hosts or zones.
optionFeedback: Two copies in one failure domain is one copy.
Rack locality buys replication latency and still loses every copy when the rack goes.
Replicas on the same host do not protect against that host failing.

variants.title: Own the key
variants.context: For one ring version, each key has deterministic primary ownership. Fenced ownership, gradual range movement, replica promotion, and warm-up controls make membership changes observable and reversible.
variants.prompt: A new node joins and immediately takes its full share of traffic. What is the risk?
options: Its cache is cold, so its misses surge at the origin.
None; the ring gives it a proportional share of keys.
It fills memory faster than the older nodes and evicts.
optionFeedback: Warm-up bounds the miss surge.
A proportional share is still a share of keys this node has never seen, so nearly every read misses.
The node starts empty, so memory pressure is the last problem it has. The cold misses land first.
variants.hint: What is the hit rate of an empty node?

variants.title: Prevent revival
variants.context: Versions and tombstones prevent delayed replicas from reviving old values. DELETE carries a version so it cannot revive an older write.
variants.prompt: A delayed replica applies an old SET after a newer DELETE. What prevents the old value from coming back?
options: A longer TTL that outlives the replication delay.
Nothing; the next write overwrites the value anyway.
A versioned tombstone that rejects the older write.
optionFeedback: TTL controls how long a value lives, not which of two writes wins.
Until that next write lands, readers see data that was deleted. That is a correctness bug, not a delay.
Versioned deletes cannot revive old values.
variants.hint: Which write is newer, and how does the replica know?
variants.explanation: DELETE(key, version) invalidates without reviving an older write.

variants.title: Prevent revival
variants.context: Versions and tombstones prevent delayed replicas from reviving old values. DELETE carries a version so it cannot revive an older write.
variants.prompt: A 3 MB object is being cached. What does the contract say?
options: Split it across three keys and reassemble on read.
Values above 1 MB belong in object storage or a CDN.
Compress it to fit and keep it in the cache anyway.
optionFeedback: Chunks expire independently, so a read can reassemble a mix of old and new parts.
Large values are out of scope.
Compression hides the size from the limit while every reader pays the decode cost. The object still does not belong here.
variants.hint: What is the value size bound?

variants.title: Prevent revival
variants.context: Versions and tombstones prevent delayed replicas from reviving old values. DELETE carries a version so it cannot revive an older write.
variants.prompt: After a node failure, a replica is promoted. What must the promotion preserve?
options: The address the failed node was reachable on.
The ring version and the versions on the values.
Nothing; the replica already holds the same values.
optionFeedback: Clients find owners through the ring, so reusing an address preserves nothing about correctness.
Promotion is a membership change with the same fencing rules.
It holds the values but not the fencing state, so a delayed write can revive data after promotion.
variants.hint: What could an old write do after promotion?
variants.explanation: Replica promotion is part of the ownership contract.
